chunks: ʿAlī, from a number of our companions, from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan and al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Rizq Allāh, from Badr, the غلام of Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan, who said:

I came to al-Jabal while I did not hold to the Imamate; I loved them as a whole, until Yazīd ibn ʿAbd Allāh died. During his illness he bequeathed that al-Shihrī al-Samand, his sword, and his belt be delivered to his Mawlā.

So I feared that if I did not hand over al-Shihrī to Idhkūtakīn, I would suffer belittlement from him. So I appraised the animal, the sword, and the belt at seven hundred dinars within myself and informed no one of it. Then a letter came to me from al-ʿIrāq: 'Send the seven hundred dinars which are due to us from you, from the price of al-Shihrī, the sword, and the belt.'

key_terms.أَوْصَى: he made a bequest during illness or before death
key_terms.الشِّهْرِيُّ: the named horse mentioned in the report
key_terms.الْإِمَامَةِ: the doctrine and authority of the Imam
key_terms.الْكِتَابُ: the written message that arrived from al-ʿIrāq
key_terms.الْمِنْطَقَةَ: the belt or girdle included with the bequeathed items
key_terms.سَبْعَ مِائَةَ دِينَارٍ: the appraised value of the items
key_terms.مَوْلَاهُ: his master, referring here to the Imam

ai.seo_question: How does this hadith present a sign of the Imam's knowledge concerning privately assessed property?
ai.summary: This hadith narrates an incident in which a man was entrusted with property to be delivered to the Imam, yet due to fear of a political authority he internally assessed its value instead. A letter then arrived from al-ʿIrāq specifying the exact amount he had privately determined, serving in the narrative as a sign connected to the Imam and the doctrine of Imamate.

en.hubeali: Ali, from a number of our companions, from Ahmad Bin Al Hassan and Al A’ala Bin Rizqillah, from Badr Ghulam Ahmad Bn Al Hassan who said,

‘I went to Al-Jabal and I was not saying (believing) in the Imamate. I loved them<sup>asws</sup> summarily until when Yazeed Bin Abdullah died, and he bequeathed to me during his illness that Shahry Al-Samand (his horse), and his sword, and his belt to be handed over to his Master<sup>asws</sup>.

But, I feared that if I do not hand over Al-Shahry (the horse) to Izkowtakeyn (a Turkish official of the Abbaside Caliph), I would be harmed from him frightfully. So I evaluated the animal, and the sword, and the belt for seven hundred Dinars within myself and did not notify anyone upon it, but the letter (from the 12<sup>th</sup> Imam<sup>asws</sup>) had arrived to me from Al-Iraq: ‘Divert (to me<sup>asws</sup>) the seven hundred Dinars which is for us<sup>asws</sup> with you from the price of Al-Shahry (the horse), and the sword, and the belt’.
en.sarwar: 15. Ali ibn Muhammad has narrated from Muhammad ibn Salih who has said the following.

“When my father died and the task (of working is representative of the Imams) was left to me with my father there were promissory notes from those who has said the following. owed (religious dues). I wrote to him (the Imam (a.s.) about the case. He wrote back to me, “Demand from them and make them pay.”

People paid what they owed except one man who had signed a promissory note for four hundred Dinars. I went to demand from him what he owed but he procrastinated and took it lightly and his behaved foolishly. I complained to his father and he said, “So what!” I then hold him by his beard and leg and pulled him towards the center of the house and kicked him many times. His son went out and cried for help from the people of Baghdad saying, “He is a Qummi, Rafidi (derogatory name for Shi‘a) he has killed my father.” From the people of Baghdad many gathered around me. I rode my equine animal and said, “Very nice of you people of Baghdad. You support the unjust against a lonely stranger. I am a man from the sunni sect and he calls me a man from Qumm and a Rafidi so that he can destroy my rights.” The narrator has said that people then turned against him and they wanted to enter his store. I then calmed them down. The signatory in the promissory note called me and set upon himself a stipulation with an oath that said, “His wife will be divorced if he did not pay his dues.” My part of the stipulation was to ask the people to leave his place.”
